n: A second acrostic dirge begins with the same cry, “How…!” This time the focus is on the Lord himself as the one who brought the disaster. He has thrown Israel’s glory from heaven to earth and did not spare even the temple, his “footstool.”

f.g: The temple or the ark of the covenant, where God’s presence was said to rest.
Probably Jerusalem and its temple, Israel’s crowning glory.

n: Without pity the Lord has swallowed up the villages of Jacob and torn down Judah’s fortresses. Kingdom and princes are “polluted”—stripped of their sacred honor.

f.g: The towns and pasture-dwellings throughout the land.
Treated as common or profane; dishonored.

n: Israel’s “horn” (her strength) is cut off. God has pulled back the protecting right hand that once fought for Israel, and his anger burns like a wildfire.

f.g: A symbol of strength and power, like the horns of a bull.

f.w: he hath drawn back his right hand

n: The Lord is pictured as an archer aiming at his own people. Those who were most precious are struck down, and his fury pours out like fire on Zion’s “tent.”

f.g: Tent or dwelling; here the city of Zion pictured as a home.

n: The shocking phrase “The Lord was as an enemy” captures the heart of the chapter. The God who once fought for Israel now seems to fight against her, multiplying her mourning.

f.w: The Lord was as an enemy

n: God has torn down his own temple as easily as someone pulls down a garden shed. Feasts, sabbaths, king, and priest—Israel’s whole system of worship and government—have been set aside.

f.w: as if it were of a garden
f.g: Like a flimsy booth or hut in a garden or vineyard.
The temple courts where Israel gathered at appointed times.

n: The Lord has rejected his altar and sanctuary. Enemy soldiers shout in the temple as loudly as worshippers once did at a festival—a bitter reversal.

f.w: they have made a noise in the house of the LORD

n: Like a builder measuring before demolition, the Lord stretched out a line to tear down Zion’s wall. Ramparts and walls are personified as mourning together.

f.w: he hath stretched out a line
f.g: A measuring line—normally used to build, here used to mark for destruction.

n: Gates are sunk in rubble, the king is in exile, the law is no longer taught, and prophets receive no vision. Losing revelation is perhaps the deepest loss of all.

f.g: Torah instruction from priests has ceased.

f.w: her prophets also find no vision from the LORD

n: The city’s elders sit silently on the ground with dust on their heads and sackcloth on their bodies—traditional signs of mourning. Young women bow their heads in grief.

f.g: Rough goat-hair cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance.

f.w: cast up dust upon their heads

n: The poet himself breaks down in tears. In Hebrew thought the liver and bowels were the seat of deep feeling; his whole inner self is poured out because children are fainting in the streets.

f.w: my liver is poured upon the earth
f.g: An idiom for utter emotional collapse.
Nursing infants.

n: A heartbreaking scene: starving children ask their mothers for food and die in their arms. The poem refuses to look away from the human cost of sin and war.

f.g: Grain (in KJV English “corn” means grain generally, not maize).

n: The poet searches for a comparison to comfort Jerusalem but finds none; her wound is as vast as the sea. “Who can heal thee?”—a question the rest of scripture answers with the Lord himself.
False prophets had promised peace instead of exposing sin. Had they called the people to repentance, the exile might have been avoided. Their messages led straight to banishment.

f.w: Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee

f.g: Prophetic oracles or messages.

n: Passersby clap, hiss, and shake their heads in mockery: is this the city once called “the perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth”?

f.w: The joy of the whole earth

n: Enemies gloat with open mouths and gnashing teeth: “We swallowed her up—this is the day we were waiting for!” (In Hebrew, verses 16 and 17 swap their expected alphabet order, as in chapters 3 and 4.)

f.g: A gesture of hatred and contempt.

n: The real explanation: the Lord has carried out what he warned long ago through Moses and the prophets. The covenant curses were not random—they were promised consequences.

f.w: he hath fulfilled his word that he had commanded in the days of old

n: The poet urges the city’s wall itself to weep day and night without rest. Turning to the Lord in tears is the beginning of hope.

f.g: The pupil of the eye; here meaning “do not let your eyes stop weeping.”

n: “Pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord.” Zion is invited to pray honestly and persistently through the night for her starving children.

f.g: The start of each night watch; ancient nights were divided into watches (three in Israelite reckoning).

f.w: lift up thy hands toward him

n: Zion speaks directly to God: look at what has happened! The famine was so terrible that mothers ate their own children, and priests and prophets were killed in the temple.

f.w: Shall the women eat their fruit

f.g: About the width of a hand—tiny infants. Some read “children they have cared for.”

n: Young and old lie dead in the streets. Jerusalem speaks with painful honesty to God, who has not held back in the day of judgment.

f.w: my virgins and my young men are fallen by the sword

n: God summoned terrors from every side as if calling worshippers to a feast day. No one escaped, and the children Zion raised were consumed—the chapter ends in raw grief.

f.g: Echoes Jeremiah’s repeated phrase magor-missabib, “terror on every side.”
Wrapped as newborns; cared for from infancy.
